primer.title: Before you read this paper
primer.overview: The paper assumes six concepts and explains none of them. The order below follows the prerequisite chain: every concept comes before the one that depends on it. Each entry gives the intuition first, then the formal definition, then exactly why this paper needs it.

dot-product.intuition: You multiply two vectors element by element and add the results. The number you get measures how much the two point in the same direction: large and positive when aligned, near zero when perpendicular, negative when opposed. It is a similarity score.
dot-product.whyItMatters: The whole of attention rests on this. How much a query attends to a key is decided by the dot product between them. That is why the paper calls its attention function "Scaled Dot-Product Attention".

softmax.intuition: You have a list of arbitrary numbers and want to turn them into positive weights that sum to one. Softmax exponentiates each and divides by the total. Large numbers take a disproportionately large share — it behaves like a soft maximum.
softmax.whyItMatters: Dot-product scores are raw numbers; softmax turns them into "how much should I look at each position" weights. Its critical behaviour is this: as the inputs grow, the output piles onto a single position and the gradients nearly vanish. That is exactly the reason the paper divides by √d_k.

variance.intuition: Variance measures how far a random value spreads from its mean. Add independent values and the variances add: sum d_k independent terms each of variance 1 and the total has variance d_k, so a standard deviation of √d_k.
variance.whyItMatters: This is the entire argument in the paper's footnote. As d_k grows the dot products typically grow on the scale of √d_k and softmax saturates. Dividing by √d_k pulls the spread back to unit scale. The scaling is not cosmetic; it follows directly from this calculation.

embedding.intuition: The model works with numbers, not words. Each token is represented by a learned vector of fixed length, tuned during training so that tokens with similar meaning land near one another.
embedding.whyItMatters: In the Transformer every sub-layer and every embedding layer must output the same dimension (512), so that residual connections can be added. This constraint shows up everywhere in the architecture.

rnn-bottleneck.intuition: In a recurrent network the hidden state at position t depends on t−1. To process word 500 you must first have finished 499. The computation is inherently queued — however many GPUs you have.
rnn-bottleneck.whyItMatters: This is why the paper exists. Because the Transformer breaks that dependency it can parallelise within a training example and reach state of the art in twelve hours on eight GPUs.

residual-layernorm.intuition: A residual connection adds a sub-layer's output back to its input: LayerNorm(x + Sublayer(x)). The layer then answers "what should I add to the current representation" rather than "produce a representation from scratch". Normalisation keeps values on a fixed scale so deep stacks stay trainable.
residual-layernorm.whyItMatters: This is why six-layer stacks train at all. The paper does not ablate either component, so their contribution is unmeasured — but without them this depth is not practical.

encoder-decoder.intuition: The encoder turns the input sequence into a sequence of representations. The decoder consults those and produces the output one token at a time, feeding each token it has generated back in as input. That is auto-regressive generation.
encoder-decoder.whyItMatters: You need this to see why masking in the decoder is mandatory: if the model can see the future during training, it comes to rely on information it will not have at inference. Masking is a correctness condition, not a speed optimisation.

deriv-scaling.title: Where dividing by √d_k comes from
deriv-scaling.goal: Derive, step by step, the scaling rationale the paper gives in a single sentence, starting from the probabilistic argument in its footnote.

s1: The starting point: the compatibility score between a query and a key is a sum of d_k terms.
s2: The paper's footnote assumption: the components are independent random variables with mean 0 and variance 1. This is an assumption, not a proof — it does not hold exactly in a trained model.
s3: Variances add for independent variables. With d_k terms the total variance is exactly d_k.
s4: Standard deviation is the square root of variance. So the typical magnitude of the scores grows with √d_k, not d_k — this is the source of the scaling factor.
s5: As the inputs grow, the exponential overwhelmingly favours the largest term. The output becomes almost one-hot, and in that region softmax has almost no gradient — what the paper calls 'extremely small gradients'.
s6: Dividing by √d_k fixes the variance at 1 regardless of d_k. Softmax then sees inputs at the same scale whatever d_k is, and does not saturate.

numericExample.setup: The paper's configuration: d_k = 64. Suppose the typical gap between two keys' scores is on the order of a standard deviation, that is √64 = 8.
walkthrough: Without scaling: a score gap of 8 → softmax weight ≈ 1/(1+e⁻⁸) ≈ 0.9997
The model is looking at essentially one position; the gradients for the others are vanishingly small.
With scaling: the gap becomes 8/√64 = 1 → softmax weight ≈ 1/(1+e⁻¹) ≈ 0.731
That is a healthy distribution producing stable gradients.
numericExample.result: At d_k = 64 the scaling pulls a single weight from 0.9997 down to 0.731. As d_k grows the unscaled version sticks to 1 while the scaled one stays constant. You can slide through this yourself in the "Why the scaling is necessary" playground.

deriv-multihead.title: How multi-head attention preserves the dimensions
deriv-multihead.goal: Show through shape tracking why splitting into h heads does not change the total cost.

m1: The input: n positions, each of dimension d_model = 512.
m2: Every head has its own projection matrices. We choose d_k = d_v = d_model/h = 512/8 = 64.
m3: Each head computes attention in a 64-dimensional subspace instead of the full dimension. Cost per head drops by a factor of 8.
m4: The critical point: h·d_v = 8·64 = 512 = d_model. Concatenating the heads brings us back to exactly the dimension we started from.
m5: The final projection mixes what the heads found. Since the dimension is unchanged, the residual connection can be added directly — the rest of the architecture notices nothing.

walkthrough: Single head at full dimension: one attention computation over 512-dimensional Q, K, V.
Multi-head: eight attention computations at 64 dimensions.
Attention cost scales linearly with dimension, so 8 × 64 = 512: the total is the same.
numericExample.result: Multi-head is not added capacity but a redistribution of the same budget. The gain comes from being able to attend to different representation subspaces at once — measured in Table 3 row (A) as 0.9 BLEU.

deriv-lrate.title: The warmup learning rate schedule
deriv-lrate.goal: Show why Equation (3) first rises and then falls, and exactly where the breakpoint sits.

l1: Equation (3) from the paper. A min of two branches: whichever is smaller applies.
l2: Early in training the second branch is selected and grows LINEARLY with step. This is what stops the model taking large steps while it is still randomly initialised.
l3: The breakpoint is exactly step = warmup — step 4000 in this work. Because the two branches are equal there, the schedule is continuous; there is no jump.
l4: After that the first branch takes over and the learning rate decays with the inverse square root of the step number — classic convergence behaviour.

play-scaling.title: Why the scaling is necessary
play-scaling.description: Slide d_k. In the unscaled version a single attention weight rushes to 1 — the region where gradients vanish. Divided by √d_k it stays constant regardless of d_k. The comparison shows the case where the score gap between two keys equals the typical spread (√d_k).
play-scaling.paperAnchor: The paper uses d_k = 64 (d_model = 512, h = 8). The scaling rationale is presented as a HYPOTHESIS ('We suspect'), not a measured result.

play-complexity.title: When self-attention becomes expensive
play-complexity.description: Run the two rows of Table 1 side by side. Self-attention is O(n²·d), a recurrent layer O(n·d²). While n < d self-attention is cheap; once n passes d the curves cross and the advantage reverses. The y-axis is logarithmic.
play-complexity.paperAnchor: The paper uses d_model = 512 and states explicitly that self-attention is faster than a recurrent layer only while n < d. The point n = d is that threshold; once the ratio passes 1 the paper's condition is violated.

sim-attention.title: Attention weights, step by step
sim-attention.description: The six steps of Scaled Dot-Product Attention. The grid shows the weight each query gives each key in a four-token sentence; darker means heavier. The numbers are ILLUSTRATIVE — the paper publishes no example attention matrix; the mechanism shown belongs to the paper, the values serve the explanation.

qkv: The input passes through three separate projections
scores: A raw compatibility score for every query-key pair
scale: Pulls the variance back to unit scale
mask: In the decoder, looking ahead is set to −∞
out: A weighted sum of the values

frames: Split the input three ways
The same input goes through three different learned projections: query (what am I looking for), key (what do I have), value (what do I give if found).
Compute the raw scores
Every query is dotted with every key. The values can grow freely — the typical spread here is on the order of √d_k.
Scale by √d_k
All scores are divided by √64 = 8. The range narrows and softmax no longer works in its saturated region.
Mask the future
In the decoder position i may only see positions before i. Forbidden cells are set to −∞ at the softmax input; shown here as 0.
Apply softmax
Each row becomes a weight distribution summing to 1. The lower-triangular structure holds: no position gives weight to the future.
Sum the values by weight
The final step: each position's output is the sum of the value vectors scaled by the weights. All of this happens for every position at once, as a single matrix multiplication — no sequentiality.

sim-encoder-decoder.title: How information flows from encoder to decoder
sim-encoder-decoder.description: The three uses of attention and where each sits in the stack. Watch which component is active at each step.

enc-in: Embedding and sinusoidal encoding are summed
enc-self: Every position may attend to all input positions
enc-ffn: Two position-wise linear transformations with ReLU in between
dec-cross: Queries from the decoder, keys and values from the encoder

frames: The input is prepared
Because there is no recurrence, order must be injected separately: sinusoidal position encodings are ADDED to the embeddings, not concatenated.
The encoder stack runs (×6)
Self-attention and the feed-forward network, each wrapped in a residual connection and layer normalisation, repeated six times. All positions are processed in parallel.
The decoder looks at its own past
Masked self-attention: position i may depend only on known outputs at positions before i. This is how auto-regression is preserved.
The decoder looks at the input
The third sub-layer: queries come from the previous decoder layer, keys and values from the encoder stack's output. This is the counterpart of classic seq2seq attention.
A token is produced
The output is turned into probabilities through weights shared with the embedding matrix. The generated token is then fed back and the loop continues.

data-table2.title: Table 2: quality and training cost
data-table2.description: The paper's WMT 2014 English-German results. Click a column header to sort. Sorting by FLOPs makes the Transformer's real claim visible: the base model takes the second-highest BLEU at the lowest cost.

quiz.title: Check your understanding
quiz.intro: Ten questions. After each answer you can see which claim and which page it rests on. The correct answers sit openly in the JSON — this is a self-check, not an exam.

q-core.prompt: What is the paper's central claim about the Transformer?
options: Dispensing with recurrence and convolution entirely and relying only on attention
The abstract's own words: 'dispensing with recurrence and convolutions entirely'.
Inventing the attention mechanism
Attention predates the paper, as Section 2 acknowledges. The novelty is making attention the sole carrier.
Showing that larger models can be trained
The emphasis is architecture rather than scale; even the base model beats its rivals at a fraction of the cost.

q-complexity.prompt: According to Table 1, what is the per-layer computational complexity of a self-attention layer?
options: O(n² · d)
Table 1, page 6. It grows with the SQUARE of the sequence length — the paper's acknowledged central trade-off.
O(n · d²)
That is the cost of a recurrent layer.
O(n log n)
No such row appears in the paper.

q-when-faster.prompt: When is self-attention faster than a recurrent layer?
options: When the sequence length n is smaller than the representation dimension d
The paper states this condition explicitly (pp. 6-7). On long contexts the condition breaks and the advantage disappears.
Always
The paper makes no such claim; it states the condition itself.
Only on GPUs
The comparison is asymptotic and hardware-independent.

q-scaling.prompt: At what evidence level does the paper justify dividing dot products by √d_k?
options: A hypothesis — the paper says 'We suspect' and offers no measurement
Page 4. The footnote gives a probabilistic motivation, but no direct comparison of scaled against unscaled is reported here.
A result measured by ablation
Table 3 ablates head count, d_k, model size and position encoding — not the scaling factor.
A mathematical theorem
The variance argument in the footnote is a motivation, not a derivation or proof.

q-heads.prompt: Which of these are true of multi-head attention?
options: It uses h = 8 heads with d_k = d_v = 64
Page 5: d_k = d_v = d_model/h = 512/8 = 64.
Total computational cost stays comparable to single-head at full dimensionality
Because the per-head dimension is divided by h, the total stays constant — the paper states this explicitly.
Increasing the head count monotonically improves quality
Table 3 row (A): with too many heads quality FALLS again. h is a hyperparameter to be tuned.
Single-head attention is 0.9 BLEU worse than the best setting
Table 3 row (A), page 9.

q-positional.prompt: Sinusoidal position encoding is measurably better than learned positional embeddings.
options: False
Table 3 row (E): the two versions give NEARLY IDENTICAL results. The sinusoidal version was preferred in the HOPE that it would generalise to longer sequences — a hope that was never tested.
True
The paper does not show this; it reports nearly identical results.

q-masking.prompt: What does masking in the decoder accomplish?
options: It guarantees the prediction at position i depends only on positions before i
Page 3. This is not a speed optimisation but a CORRECTNESS condition for auto-regressive generation.
It reduces memory
Masking sets forbidden entries to −∞ at the softmax input; memory is not the goal.
It speeds up training
The goal is not speed but preventing the model from seeing the future.

q-cost.prompt: How were the training-cost (FLOPs) figures in Table 2 obtained?
options: Estimated: time × GPU count × assumed capacity per GPU
Page 8. These are estimates, not measurements; adequate for comparing orders of magnitude but not small differences.
Measured directly with a profiler
The paper performs no such measurement.
Taken from the hardware vendor's report
The capacity figures are given as assumptions in a footnote; the costs are computed by the authors.

q-restricted.prompt: The restricted self-attention proposed for long sequences was measured in this paper.
options: False
Page 7: 'We plan to investigate this approach further in future work.' There is a proposal, but no measurement.
True
It has a row in Table 1 but no experimental result is reported.

q-generalization.prompt: What evidence of generalisation beyond translation does the paper offer?
options: English constituency parsing: a 4-layer model reaching 92.7 F1 in the semi-supervised setting
Table 4, page 10. Obtained without task-specific tuning; it is the only additional task.
Image classification
There is no vision experiment here; it appears only as a future plan in the conclusion.
Language modelling
The paper reports no language modelling result.

applicationGuide.title: Using it in your own project
applicationGuide.overview: You do not need to write a Transformer from scratch today. But knowing why each decision was made changes how you pick your own configuration. Every value below comes from the paper — there are no invented defaults. The code sketches are EXPLANATORY, not runnable library code.
recipe: Choose d_model first, then h so that it divides evenly. Preserve the relation d_k = d_v = d_model/h; break it and the total cost no longer stays constant, which invalidates any comparison with the paper's ablations.
Tie the scaling to d_k, do not hard-code it
The 1/√d_k factor depends on d_k. Change the head dimension and the scaling must change with it; a hard-coded 0.125 (that is, 1/√64) turns into a silent bug.
Put the mask INSIDE the attention function
Masking is not zeroing after softmax. Forbidden connections must be set to −∞ at the softmax INPUT; zero them afterwards and the rows no longer sum to 1 and the weights are wrong.
Use the warmup learning rate schedule

Training a Transformer with a fixed learning rate is a classic failure mode. Equation (3) rises linearly for the first warmup_steps and then decays with step^-0.5; the breakpoint is exactly step = warmup.
Select checkpoints on BLEU, not perplexity

Label smoothing deliberately hurts perplexity. The paper says so outright: 'This hurts perplexity ... but improves accuracy and BLEU score.' Pick your best checkpoint by validation perplexity and you will pick the wrong model.
hyperparameters: Table 3 row (C): dropping to 256 takes BLEU from 25.8 to 24.5; raising to 1024 lifts it to 26.0. Bigger helps, with diminishing returns.
A single head costs 0.9 BLEU; 32 heads also degrade. The band between 8 and 16 works best. Not monotonic — tune it.
Usually taken as 4·d_model. Raising it to 4096 lifts BLEU to 26.2 but pushes the parameter count to 90M.

This value is given as a single setting and never swept. If your total step count differs greatly from 100K, consider scaling proportionally — but the paper offers no basis for that, so measure it on your own validation set.
Table 3 row (D): turning dropout off takes BLEU from 25.8 to 24.6. Smaller datasets may need a higher value.
pitfalls: Training diverges or the loss becomes NaN in the first few thousand steps
A fixed learning rate with no warmup. The model takes large steps while still randomly initialised.
Apply the warmup schedule from Equation (3); the learning rate should rise linearly over the first 4000 steps.
Attention weights are almost one-hot and the model is not learning
The √d_k scaling is missing or tied to the wrong dimension. Scores grow on the order of √d_k and push softmax into saturation.
Tie the scaling to d_k. You can see the effect by sliding d_k in the "Why the scaling is necessary" playground.
Validation perplexity improves while BLEU falls
Label smoothing hurts perplexity by design; the two metrics do not move together.
Select checkpoints by BLEU, as the paper does.
Memory blows up on long documents
Self-attention costs O(n²·d). The paper's advantage condition (n < d) is violated in long contexts.
The paper proposes restricted attention for this case but never measures it. In practice look at chunking, sparse attention, or the efficient-attention variants developed after this paper.
My ablation numbers do not match the paper's
Table 3 was measured on the development set (newstest2013) WITHOUT checkpoint averaging; Table 2 was measured on the test set with averaging.
Check which table you are comparing against. The two are not directly comparable, and the paper warns about this explicitly.
whenNotToUse: When the sequence length markedly exceeds the representation dimension: the paper's own analysis says self-attention loses its advantage over a recurrent layer in that regime.
On very small datasets without task-specific tuning: the paper notes that even its parsing experiments involved only a small number of hyperparameter trials.

When sequential generation latency is critical: the Transformer parallelises training, but inference still emits one token at a time — the paper leaves 'making generation less sequential' to future work.
When carrying the paper's numbers to another model family: all results are specific to 2017 hardware and these datasets, and the FLOP estimates do not hold on today's hardware.
